fixes.explanation: That's the line, friend. The proverb says "Every wise woman builds her house, but a foolish one tears it down with her own hands." The wise woman builds her house. The foolish one tears hers down, and she does it with her own hands.
No neighbor shows up in this proverb at all. The foolish woman's hands are busy with something else. The text says she "…tears it down with her own hands." Tearing down, not handing over.

It's true, friend. The proverb says the upright man fears the LORD, "…but the one who is devious in his ways despises Him." So the devious man is the one who despises the LORD. Easy one to doubt when you read it fast.

That's it, friend. "The proud speech of a fool brings a rod to his back…" His own mouth sends the bill. The same verse says the lips of the wise protect them, so a mouth can be a shield or a problem, depending on whose it is.

That's the word, friend. The verse says "Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty, but an abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox." No oxen means an empty manger. The harvest is what comes through the ox's strength.

Dust is a fair guess, friend, but the verse never mentions it. The proverb says "…an abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox." The empty manger belongs to the side with no oxen. The harvest comes through the ox.

That's what the text says: "A mocker seeks wisdom and finds none…" He goes looking and comes back with empty hands. Meanwhile, "…knowledge comes easily to the discerning." Easy for one, none for the other.

Plenty is a big hope for the mocker, friend, but the proverb says he "…seeks wisdom and finds none…" Finding none is the opposite of finding plenty. The other half of the verse says "…knowledge comes easily to the discerning."

Yes, friend. The verse says "The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools deceives them." So the prudent man discerns his way, and the fool gets deceived by his own folly. Getting fooled by your own folly is a rough way to get got.
The proverb doesn't name a brother here, friend. It says "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy." The word is stranger. A brother just isn't in the verse.
No servant in this one, friend. The line is "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy." Stranger is the word the verse uses. Servant isn't anywhere in it.

That's right, friend. The verse says "The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish." So the wicked man's house is the one that comes down. The upright man's tent is the one that flourishes.

That's what the verse says: "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death." It's a heavy line, and I'll let it be heavy. A way can seem right, and the verse still tells you where it ends.
Yes, friend. The proverb says "The simple man believes every word, but the prudent man watches his steps." The simple man takes in every word. The prudent man is busy watching his steps.

Forgetting would be a different problem, friend. The proverb says the simple man "…believes every word…" Forgetting a word and swallowing every word are two different troubles. The prudent man is the one who "…watches his steps."

Cautious is a good word, friend, but the proverb doesn't use it. It says the wise man "…fears and turns from evil…" and the fool is "…careless and reckless." Cautious is nearly the opposite of what the fool is called there.
That's the first blank, friend. The proverb says "A quick-tempered man acts foolishly…" A short fuse gets its label right there in the verse. The label is foolishly.

That's the second blank, friend. The proverb says "A quick-tempered man acts foolishly, and a devious man is hated." Hated is the word the verse gives the devious man. Sneaky doesn't win people over, I'd say.
Trusted sounds nice, friend, but the text says "…a devious man is hated." I bet a devious man would like a better word. Hated is the word the verse uses, though.

Honored isn't the word the proverb uses, friend. It says "…a devious man is hated." The king delighting in a wise servant shows up later (Proverbs 14:35), but that's a different verse about a different kind of person.

Yes, friend, that one is false. The verse says "The evil bow before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous." The evil are the ones who bow before the good. So the bowing runs the other way.

Yes, friend. The verse says "…those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness." Planning goodness is the work, and devotion and faithfulness are what they find. The ones who contrive evil, the verse says, go astray.
That's right, it's false. The proverb says "There is profit in all labor, but mere talk leads only to poverty." Notice it says all labor. Talking about the work isn't doing the work, friend.

Yes, friend. The proverb says "He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge." The man who fears the LORD is secure in confidence. His children shall have a place of refuge.

The proverb says it's true, friend. "He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge." The verse says his children shall have a place of refuge. So that part stands.

The praise of men doesn't show up in this verse, friend. It says the fear of the LORD is "…a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death." Nobody's applause is in there. The snares of death are the thing it turns him from.
Yes, friend. The proverb says "A large population is a king’s splendor, but a lack of subjects is a prince’s ruin." Splendor goes with a large population. Ruin goes with a lack of subjects.

Joy isn't the word, friend. The proverb says "A large population is a king’s splendor, but a lack of subjects is a prince’s ruin." Splendor is on the large-population side. A lack of subjects gets ruin.
The proverb doesn't call him slow, friend. It says "A patient man has great understanding…" The quick-tempered man is the one who "promotes folly." So patience sits on the understanding side.
Right, friend. The proverb says "A patient man has great understanding…" Patient and slow aren't the same thing. It's the quick-tempered man who "promotes folly."
That's the one, friend: "…envy rots the bones." The verse sets it right beside "A tranquil heart is life to the body…" It's an ugly word for an ugly thing.

Kindness is a good word, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The text says "A tranquil heart is life to the body, but envy rots the bones." The verse sets a tranquil heart against envy. Envy is the one named as rotting the bones.

That's the word, friend. "Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker…" The proverb ties how a person treats the poor to the One who made them. And the same verse says "…whoever is kind to the needy honors Him."
The proverb says the opposite, friend. "Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker…" Pleasing isn't the word the verse uses. It's the one who is kind to the needy who "honors Him."
Serving is a nice word, friend, but the proverb doesn't use it there. The text says "Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker…" Whoever is kind to the needy is the one who honors Him.
Yes, friend. The verse says "The wicked man is thrown down by his own sin, but the righteous man has a refuge even in death." Even in death, the verse says. That's the part to hold onto.
That's the first blank, friend. The proverb says "Righteousness exalts a nation…" It lifts a nation up. Exalts is the word that fills it.
That's the second blank, friend. The proverb says "…sin is a disgrace to any people." Righteousness exalts a nation, and sin is a disgrace to any people.
Divides sounds like trouble for a nation, friend, but it's not the word the proverb uses. It says "Righteousness exalts a nation…" That's the lifting-up word the blank is after.

Yes, friend. The verse says "A king delights in a wise servant, but his anger falls on the shameful." The wise servant gets the king's delight. The shameful get his anger, and I know which one I'd rather get.

Favor is a good guess, friend, but it's not what the verse says falls on the shameful. The proverb says "A king delights in a wise servant, but his anger falls on the shameful." Delight is for the wise servant. Anger is what falls on the shameful.
